article.title: Lifetime of Education
article.author: Peter McLaren
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. I was born in 1948, into a world that had only recently emerged from the catastrophe of the Second World War. I was an only child. My father had served with the Royal Canadian Engineers, and after the war he needed time to recover from the experiences he had endured. The war did not simply end when the guns fell silent. It remained in the memories of those who had survived it, in the silences of families, and in the difficult business of learning how to live again. My uncle, who visited us on weekends, had been involved in the Allied action that sank the German battleship Bismarck. I grew up with these fragments of wartime history, not always fully understanding their meaning, but knowing that the world into which I had been born had come perilously close to destroying itself. The adults around me had witnessed something that no generation should have to witness again. I inherited from them a hope that the world might somehow learn from its own devastation—that another world conflagration could be prevented. I have carried that hope throughout my life. It has never been an uncomplicated optimism. The history of the twentieth century offered too many reasons for skepticism, and the twenty-first has supplied more than enough of its own. Yet I have remained attached to the belief that human beings are capable of making a world other than the one they have inherited. That conviction would eventually become the animating principle of my work in education, critical pedagogy, and political writing. Perhaps this is one reason I have never understood education as merely the transmission of information, the preparation of individuals for employment, or the cultivation of credentials. Education is implicated in the formation of the world itself. It can reproduce the arrangements of power that already exist, teaching people to accommodate themselves to injustice; or it can help cultivate the historical imagination necessary to challenge those arrangements. The question that has accompanied me from the classroom to the university, from Toronto to the United States and beyond, has been deceptively simple: What might human beings become if they were not required to accept the limits imposed upon them? Toronto: The Beginniings of a Critical Imagination My intellectual life began long before I acquired the language with which to describe it. Growing up in Toronto, I was fortunate to find myself among friends who were essayists, musicians, and poets. We were young, curious, and drawn toward the possibilities of language and artistic expression. Intellectual life did not yet have the institutional form of a university seminar or academic conference. It was something we made among ourselves—in conversation, argument, reading, and the restless search for a larger world. One of my friends, whom I shall call Jack, was the most brilliant among us. He possessed an extraordinaryintellectual energy. Our friendships belonged to a period of discovery, when ideas seemed capable of opening doors into entirely different ways of living. As the years passed, however, Jack's life took a difficult direction, and I gradually came to understand that I needed to find my own path. Leaving Toronto for university was part of that process. It was not a repudiation of the friendships that had shaped me, but an attempt to discover what kind of intellectual life might become possible beyond the familiar boundaries of home. Related: Trump, the Imperial Presidency, and the Perilous Future of the Republic I went to the University of Waterloo, where I studied Shakespearean drama. Shakespeare offered an education in the contradictions of human existence: ambition and conscience, authority and rebellion, love and betrayal, the comedy of human folly and the tragedy of historical consequence. His characters inhabit worlds in which power is never merely external. It enters the imagination, shapes desire, and becomes entangled with the stories people tell themselves about who they are. I did not yet have a fully developed theory of ideology or social reproduction, but I was learning to recognize the political dimensions of human experience. I later pursued a master's degree at Brock University. By then, I had already published Cries from the Corridor, a book drawn from my experiences as an elementary schoolteacher in Toronto's Jane-Finch Corridor. I had taught children across the elementary grades, from Grade 2 toGrade6, in a community widely associated with high-rise housing, poverty, and violence. But the children I encountered were never reducible to the public descriptions of their neighbourhood. They possessed imagination, humour, intelligence, vulnerability, and a capacity for human possibility that the surrounding social conditions too often denied them. The book became a Canadian bestseller, reaching number seven on the national bestseller list. Its success was gratifying, but what mattered most to me was that the lives of children and teachers who were ordinarily absent from the country's preferred narratives had entered public conversation. Cries from the Corridorwas subsequently developed as a film project for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. At the last moment, however, production was halted because of a technicians' strike, or so I was told. The film was never made. I have never entirely abandoned the feeling that it may yet be made, long after I am gone. Perhaps some stories refuse to accept the finality of their postponement. The material of Cries from the Corridor later found a place in Life in Schools. The classroom had become more than the setting for my professional life. It had become a site from which to examine the larger organization of society: the unequal distribution of opportunity, the cultural assumptions embedded in schooling, and the ways in which institutions can either affirm or diminish the lives of those entrusted to them. My subsequent doctoral work at the Ontario Institute for Studies in Education deepened my engagement with the relationship between education, ritual, culture, and social power. I was increasingly drawn toward the understanding that schools are not isolatedinstitutions. They are connected to the economic, political, and cultural arrangements of the societies in which they exist. The classroom is never entirely separate from the world outside it. In 1968, I hitchhiked and traveled by Greyhound bus from Toronto to San Francisco, drawn westward by the extraordinary cultural upheavals of the decade. San Francisco had become a symbolic geography of rebellion, a place where the conventions of respectable society seemed to be dissolving into experiments with consciousness, communal living, music, and the possibilities of personal liberation. I arrived as a young Canadian eager to discover what lay beyond the familiar boundaries of my upbringing. One evening, at the Carousel Ballroom, later known as the Fillmore West, I noticed a man sitting across from me who was staring at me intently. I recognized him immediately. It was Timothy Leary, the controversial psychologist whose experiments with psychedelic consciousness had made him one of the most recognizable figures of the counterculture. Eventually, Leary approached me. He produced several purple pills, which we both consumed, and what followed was a night of extraordinarily intense conversation. I cannot pretend to reconstruct everything we discussed. What remains with me is the peculiar intimacy of that encounter, the sensation of two strangers inhabiting, for a few hours, a world in which the ordinary boundaries of perception and conversation seemed to have become strangely permeable. Related: Elbows Up! Canada, Trump, and the Politics of Democratic Friendship At some point during the evening, Leary took out a piece of paper, scribbled something upon it, and handed it to me. I slipped the note into my pocket. Later, making my way back to a rooming house crowded with hippies, I unfolded the paper and read what hehad written: “You are now free! —Timothy Leary.” I have often thought about those words in the decades since. At the time, they belonged to a cultural moment in which freedom was frequently imagined as an emancipation of consciousness from the prohibitions of conventional society. But the years that followed would compel me to ask a more demanding question: What does it mean to be free in a world where the material conditions of human existence remain structured by exploitation, inequality, and domination? I had traveled to San Francisco searching, perhaps without fully knowing it, for an enlargement of the possible. Leary handed me a sentence. History would require me to spend the rest of my life interrogating its meaning. Henry Giroux and the Music of Intellectual Life My intellectual development took a decisive turn through my association with Henry Giroux. By the time I encountered him as a graduate student, Henry was already a formidable intellectual presence. He had an extraordinary capacity to make ideas move. His lectures were not simply presentations of arguments; they were performances of intellectual possibility. Concepts seemed to gather momentum as he spoke, each proposition opening into another, his language forceful, inventive, and almost musical. Henry Giroux I later had the good fortune to work alongside him at Miami University of Ohio. My office was directly adjacent to the classroom in which Henry taught. Because I was born deaf in one ear, I would sometimes leave my office door slightly ajar so that I couldhear him more clearly.1I found myself listening to his lectures even when I was supposed to be attending to my own work. His intellectual energy was infectious. I sometimes tried to imitate his manner of speaking in my own classes. The attempt was not always successful. Henry had grown up in Smith Hill, Rhode Island, and his voice carried the rhythms of that experience. He had once operated a shoeshine stand in anAfrican American district, and he brought to his intellectual life an extraordinary sensitivity to the cultural and political textures of working-class existence. When I attempted to reproduce his delivery, I occasionally found myself speaking with something approaching a Rhode Island accent. It was a humbling reminder that intellectual style cannot simply be borrowed. But what I admired most about Henry was not his rhetorical brilliance. It was his insistence that education had to be understood as a political and cultural practice. His work helped me see more clearly that pedagogy takes place far beyond the boundaries of formal schooling. Television, popular culture, political rhetoric, public institutions, and the everyday circulation of ideas all participate in teaching people how to understand the world. Politics itself is pedagogical. It forms identities, produces common sense, and establishes the limits of what people regard as possible. Henry's influence helped me develop a more expansive understanding of critical pedagogy. Education could not be confined to questions of curriculum, classroom method, or institutional reform. It had to address the forces that shape consciousness and organize social life. It had to ask whose interests were served by prevailing arrangements and whose experiences were excluded from the stories through which a society understood itself. Our intellectual conversations, along with those I shared with many other colleagues, helped make the years at Miami among the most invigorating of my academic life. I learned that scholarship at its best is not a solitary accumulation of knowledge. It is a conversation that changes the participants. It requires disagreement, generosity, intellectual courage, and the willingness to be unsettled. Along with the works of Henry Giroux, I have admired the work of Joe Kincheloe, Antonia Darder, Donaldo Macedo, Paul R. Carr, Juha Suoranta,and many other contemporary educators. A growing group of scholars and activists continue to expand Freirean scholarship, values,and education around the world. Professor Carr is one of those leading and cultivating this field, along with international scholars such as Juha Suoranta of Finland. UCLA and the International Life of Critical Pedagogy My years at UCLA, where I served from 1992 to 2012, extended this intellectual journey into a much wider international conversation. I continued to work on critical pedagogy, Marxist social theory, cultural studies, and the relationship between education and the political economy of capitalism. I became increasingly convinced that the problems confronting education could not be understood through educational theory alone. Schools are shaped by economic structures, state policies, histories of colonialism, racialized forms of power, and the changing organization of labour. The production of knowledge is inseparable from the production of social relations. To speak of educational possibility without examining the material conditions that constrain it is to risk turning hope into an abstraction. My work brought me into contact with scholars, educators, and activists across national boundaries. I spoke at universities in Colombia during the period of my engagement with Venezuela, and I participated in conversations about popular education, revolutionary movements, and the possibilities and contradictions of emancipatory politics. These encounters challenged any temptation to regard critical pedagogy as a theory belonging to a single country or academic tradition. Its questions were international because the struggles to which it responded were international. My engagement with Venezuela was particularly important in this regard. It compelled me to consider the relationship between educational transformation and the broader political aspirations of movements seeking to challenge entrenched inequalities. Such experiences also reinforced the need for critical distance. No political project should be exempt from scrutiny simply because it speaks in the language of emancipation. A critical pedagogy worthy of the name must remain attentive to contradictions wherever they arise, including within movements with which one feels an intellectual or political affinity. I became more convinced that the task of the critical educator is neither to romanticize resistance nor to surrender to cynicism. It is to understand the historical forces at work, to recognize the possibilities emerging within them, and to help cultivate the intellectual and ethical capacities required for democratic transformation. Mexico, Instituto McLaren, and Latin America One of the most consequential developments in my intellectual life was my involvement with Instituto McLaren de Pedagogía Críticain Ensenada, Baja California, Mexico. The institution represented something more significant than the extension of my academic work into another national setting. It embodied an aspiration that had animated my scholarship for decades: critical pedagogy might cease to exist primarily as an academic discourse and become a living educational practice, grounded in the historical struggles of communities seeking to transform the conditions of their existence. The origins of this undertaking were closely associated with the Mexican educator Sergio Quiroz Miranda, whose intellectual commitment and organizational vision were indispensable to its development. Instituto McLaren emerged in 2011 as a home for sustained conversation among educators, students, and intellectuals about education, capitalism, democracy, and human emancipation. I remain grateful to colleagues who have sustained the work of the Instituto, including Rosalinda Villa Tapia. With Aleida, Che's daughter. On a trip to Cuba, I was given a tour of Che Guevara's living quarters and belongings by Che's daughter, Aleida. I became very emotional during our meeting. Recently my book, Che Guevara, Paulo Freire and Pedagogy of Revolution, was named by Bloomsbury Press as an Education Classic. Critical pedagogy could not simply be exported from North American universities into Latin America as a finished theoretical product. It had to be reconsidered through encounters with Mexican society, its revolutionary traditions, Indigenous struggles, economic inequalities, colonial inheritances, and the continuing contest over the meaning of democracy. My encounters with the Purépecha community of Cherán, Michoacán,further deepened my understanding of education as a practice inseparable from collective self-determination: the defense of communal life, cultural memory, and political autonomy. Among the most transformative experiences of my years in Mexico were my encounters with Indigenous communities in Cheránas well asthe Copper Canyon region of Chihuahua. These encounters unsettled assumptions I had carried from the intellectual traditions of Europe and North America. They compelled me to reconsider difference not simply as a category of cultural identity, but as a challenge to the presumed universality of Western understandings of knowledge, history, community, and freedom .I came to appreciate that difference is not something to be overcome on the road toward emancipation, nor merely an aesthetic expression of diversity. The Indigenous communities I encountered were not illustrations of theoretical propositions I had alreadydeveloped. They possessed their own histories, intellectual traditions, struggles, and understandings of collective existence. To treat their experiences as confirmation of my existing commitments would have reproduced the epistemological arrogance that critical pedagogy seeks to challenge. These encounters taught me that solidarity requires more than agreement. It demands a willingness to recognize the limits of one’s understanding, to listen without assuming the authority to interpret everything one hears, and to acknowledge that liberationcannot be organized around a single historical experience. I had traveled to Mexico with a language of emancipation. I returned with a deeper understanding of the necessity of listening. During my visits to Colombia, I encountered educators and students whose dedication to education and social justice left a lasting impression upon me. I was especially moved to learn that a school building in Neiva, Colombia,bore my name. I regarded this as an extraordinary honor, one that filled me with gratitude and a sense of humility. I have never forgotten the generosity of those who extended this kindness to me, nor the warmth of the students and educators I encountered there. It remains among the most touching memories of my years in Latin America. Mexico, Venezuela, Cuba, and Colombia taught me that the geography of critical pedagogy is not defined by the locations of prestigious universities. It is constituted wherever people struggle to understand the historical forces that govern their lives and to acquire the collectivecapacity to transform them. These encounters did not merely confirm my theoretical commitments; they challenged and enlarged them. Venezuela: Critical Pedagogy and Education of Hope Among the most consequential experiences of my intellectual and political life were my visits to Venezuela during the presidency of Hugo Chávez. I had been invited by members of the Venezuelan educational administration to help introduce critical pedagogy and the work of Paulo Freire into the country's educational landscape. What began as an invitation to share ideas soon became something far more profound: an encounter with a society struggling to imagine the relationship between education, political sovereignty, and the possibility of transforming everyday life. I was flown to towns and communities throughout Venezuela, where, with the indispensable assistance of translators, I spoke with educators, students, and community members about Freire's understanding of education as a practice of freedom. My travels also took me by bus to factories, where I encountered workerswhose experiences invited me to reconsider the relationship between intellectual labor and the material conditions of production. I participated in marches through the streets of Caracas, surrounded by people for whom political participation was not an abstraction confined to academic discourse but a collective expression of hope, grievance, solidarity, and historical aspiration. These encounters brought me face to face with the contradictions and possibilities of a society attempting to translate revolutionary ideals into the difficult substance of everyday existence. During my visits, I met President Hugo Chávez, who invited me to attend two broadcasts of his television program Aló Presidente! The broadcasts brought together scholars, public officials, workers, and members of local communities in an unusual form of televised political conversation. At one of these broadcasts, I had the extraordinary opportunity to meet Ernesto Cardenal, the Nicaraguan priest, philosopher, revolutionary, and poet whose life and writings embodied the encounter between Christian liberation theology and the struggle for social emancipation.For someone whose own intellectual journey would increasingly bring Freirean pedagogy into conversation with Christian spirituality and liberation theology, this meeting carried a significance that extended well beyond the occasion itself. With Ernesto Cardenal My time in Venezuela was an exceedingly important learning experience. I arrived with theoretical commitments forged through years of scholarship and political engagement, but I departed with a deeper appreciation of the complexity of revolutionary transformation. I learned that critical pedagogy cannot simply be transported from the university into the streets, factories, and classrooms of another country as though it were a finished intellectual system. It must be recreated through dialogue with the histories, cultural traditions, material struggles, and aspirations of the people themselves. Venezuela taught me that the educator who arrives prepared only to teach has already misunderstood the meaning of Freire's revolutionary humanism. To teach in solidarity is first to learn how to listen. Those experiences enlarged my understanding of critical pedagogy as an unfinished historical project, one whose possibilities and contradictions must be encountered in the lived struggles of ordinary people. They remain among the most formative experiencesof my academic life. Chapman and the Living Legacy of Paulo Freire My years at Chapman University, from 2013 to 2023, brought another important chapter in this intellectual journey. Chapman offered a community in which the legacy of Paulo Freire was not simply commemorated but actively discussed, interpreted, and extended. Tom Wilson, Suzanne SooHoo, Anaida Colón-Muñiz, and Lilia Monzó were among the colleagues whose knowledge of Freire's work helped sustain this intellectual environment. A substantial group of doctoral students was also deeply versed in Freirean thought. Other professors joined meetings, presentations,and conversations, creating a community that extended beyond any single department or discipline. The presence of Freire was made tangible by a beautiful bust of him on the Chapman campus. It became a gathering place and a point of recognition for visitors and scholars. People enjoyed having their photographs taken beside it, including Freire's wife, Nita Freire. The bust was more than a monument. It represented a living intellectual commitment to dialogue, critical consciousness, and the conviction that education could participate in the transformation of society. I found something deeply meaningful in this relationship between memory and practice. Universities often commemorate intellectual figures by placing their names on buildings or their likenesses in prominent locations. Such gestures can become exercises in institutional self-congratulation. But Freire's presence at Chapman invited a more demanding question: what does it mean to honouran educator whose work insists that we must continually question the conditions under which human beings are permitted to live, learn, and speak? The Paulo Freire Democratic Project helped keep that question alive. Its work brought together faculty, students, scholars, and community participants in an ongoing conversation about democratic education and social justice. I was privileged to contribute to this intellectual community, including through my work as a co-director and international ambassador for global ethics and social justice.What mattered was not simply the preservation of Freire's legacy, but its continued development. Freire's work had never been intended as a closed system. Its deepest lesson was the necessity of dialogue with changing historical circumstances. To invoke Freire while refusing to examine the world anew would be to misunderstand him. With Sheila Macrine During this time I had the privilege of meeting Professor Sheila Macrine. Sheila is currently a Professor in the Department of STEM Education and Teacher Development at the University of Massachusetts, Dartmouth where she coordinates the special education program. Her teaching and mentoring have been recognized with the Kappa Delta Excellence in Teaching & Advising Award. She has served on the Freire SIG of the AERA and provided me with new insights regarding teaching and learning.Meeting Professors Mike Cole, Glenn Rikowski and Dave Hill have helped me to understand education in the European political context, especially in the United Kingdom. I have enjoyed our conversations and learned much from them. China and the Expanding Conversation China came toward the end of my Chapman years, adding another dimension to the international character of my intellectual life. Encounters with Chinese scholars, writers, and educators enlarged my sense of the different historical experiences through whichquestions of education, culture, and human possibility are understood. Fengyun Wei Among the people I came to know was the Chinese author Fengyun Wei, whom I know as Joy. Her book on my educational thought, published by China Social Sciences Press, has been a moving example of the ways ideas are reinterpreted across languages and cultures. Such encounters reminded me that intellectual life is sustained not only by published theories and formal academic institutions, but also by conversations that cross linguistic and cultural boundaries. They require humility. One must be willing to listen, to recognize the limits of one's own interpretive habits, and to understand that the world cannot be adequately described from a single intellectual or national vantage point. My international experiences have never persuaded me that the differences among societies are insignificant. They have persuaded me of the opposite: that historical differences matter profoundly, and that genuine intellectual exchange requires attending to them. The task is not to erase difference in the name of an abstract universality, but to discover how people situated in different histories might nevertheless participate in a shared struggle for dignity, justice, and democratic possibility. Toward a Critical Prophetic Pedagogy My understanding of critical pedagogy has continued to change. I have moved through what I would describe as three related formulations: critical pedagogy, revolutionary critical pedagogy, and, more recently, critical prophetic pedagogy. These are not three unrelated intellectual positions, nor do I regard the later formulation as a repudiation of the earlier ones. Each represents an effort to deepen the ethical, political, and historical dimensions of the work. Critical pedagogy taught me to examine the relationship between knowledge and power, to question the apparent neutrality of educational institutions, and to recognize the ways in which ideology becomes embedded in everyday life. Revolutionary critical pedagogy extended this analysis by insisting that critique must confront the structural organization of society, including the relations of capitalism that shape education, labour, and human existence. It was not enough to interpret injustice. One had to consider the historical conditions through which it might be transformed. My more recent work also incorporates the insights of Catholic social justice educators, including José Porfirio Miranda. My correspondence with Professor James D. Kirylo has helped deepen my understanding of Catholic theology and its relationship to critical educational thought. These conversations have encouraged me to engage more seriously with liberation theology and its advances, particularly the insistence that faith cannot be separated from the historical lives of people who endure poverty, exploitation, and political violence. This engagement has helped me understand that the prophetic dimension of critical pedagogy is not an ornamental spiritual addition to political critique. It concerns the ethical responsibility to speak against injustice, to defend human dignity, and to refuse the normalization of suffering. Liberation theology has opened a way of thinking about faith as a resource for historical resistance rather than passive accommodation. It has also encouraged me to consider how love, solidarity, and compassion might be understood not as private sentiments alone but as demands upon public life. Critical prophetic pedagogy, as I understand it, does not ask educators to abandon rigorous analysis in favour of religious consolation. Nor does it ask them to surrender their critical judgment to ecclesiastical authority. It asks us to consider whether critique can be joined to a deeper ethical commitment to the lives of others, especially those whose suffering is rendered invisible by the ordinary operations of power. My spiritual journey has also been enriched by the intellectual and spiritual insights of the Jesuit David Clifton Robinson. Through my reflections upon his counsel, I have found myself drawn more deeply into questions that cannot be answered by political theory alone. At times, I have taken refuge in his friendship, discovering a companionship that has sustained me through periods of uncertainty and vulnerability. Three heart attacks have brought me into an increasingly intimate confrontation with my own mortality. I can no longer take for granted that I will awaken the following morning. The future, which once stretched before me as an apparently inexhaustible landscape of intellectual projects and personal possibilities, has become something more fragile and infinitely more precious. Questions of forgiveness, reconciliation, compassion, and grace acquire an urgency that no scholarly argument can adequately convey. I do not imagine that suffering automatically confers wisdom. Illness can leave us frightened and painfully aware of our limitations. But it can also make the ordinary miracles of existence more visible: a conversation with a friend, an unexpected act of kindness, the quiet consolation of prayer, the simple and astonishing fact of another morning. Justice without compassion risks becoming another form of domination; compassion without justice risks becoming an accommodation to suffering. The challenge is tohold them together. More recently, I have begun reading the ancient writings collectively known as the Books of Enoch, particularly the collection preserved in Ethiopia. I find myself wrestling with a question that is historical, theological, and pedagogical: why did these writings, which influenced early Jewish and Christian religious imagination, remain outside the biblical canon inherited by the translators of the King James Bible, while retaining scriptural authority within Ethiopian Christianity? The King James translators did not themselves remove Enoch; they inherited a tradition in which it was not canonical. The history of Enoch reminds me that the transmission of religious knowledge is inseparable from the communities that preserve it. Here, unexpectedly, my theological investigations intersect with what I learned from Indigenous communities in Mexico: no single intellectual tradition possesses an exhaustive vocabulary for understanding the human condition. I regard these inquiries not as a departure from critical pedagogy, but as part of my effort to understand critical prophetic pedagogy, in which historical critique, ethical responsibility, and spiritual inquiry remain in conversation. The prophetic is not a prediction of the future. It is a refusal to accept injustice as the final word in history. It names the present truthfully while insisting that the present is not all that can be. In this sense, critical prophetic pedagogy remains connected to the revolutionary aspirations of critical education while enlarging its ethical and spiritual horizon. I have also been invited to review The Story of Everything, a film by Stephen C. Meyer, author of Return of the God Hypothesis. The film is a Sypher Studios production in association with Mews Films. I have read much of Meyer’s work and followed his public debates online. Intellectual curiosity, for me, continues to require serious engagement with arguments that emerge from traditions different from my own.As a practicing Catholic,I find many of Meyer’s scientific engagements affirming theism to be convincing. The Work That Remains Retirement has changed the circumstances of my intellectual life, but it has not ended it. I spend much of my time reading, thinking, and challenging myself. I am also living with the consequences of serious cardiac episodes and vestibular problems that affect my one functioning ear. These experiences have made the body's vulnerability less theoretical than it once seemed. They have also required me to reconsider how I use my time and energy. At age 78, I have become aware of changes in my memory. I have begun turning down invitations to speak, not because I have lost interest in intellectual exchange, but because public speaking now asks something of me that I cannot always confidently promise. There are losses in this adjustment. I miss the classroom, the conference, the exchange of ideas in a room full of people who are willing to be challenged. Yet I have not relinquished the work. I continue to write regularly for LA Progressive , contributing columns and essays on current events, American politics, authoritarianism, education, and the wider struggles over democracy and human possibility. These writings have become my way of remaining in conversation with the world. They allow me to bring the critical perspectives developed over a lifetime into the political arguments of the present, to reflect on events as they unfold, and to resist the temptation to regard the crises of our time as distant or inevitable. I write because the world still demands interpretation, and because interpretation, when joined to ethical responsibility, can become a form of participation. I write because the struggle over the meaning of democracy is also a struggle over the education of desire: over what people learn to fear, what they are encouraged to accept, what they are taught to forget, and what they might yet imagine together. The present moment gives this work an urgency I could scarcely have anticipated when I was growing up in postwar Toronto. I am increasingly troubled by the possibility that the conflicts and political antagonisms of our time could lead to another world war. The prospect of nuclear confrontation, once associated in my imagination with the terrible warnings of an earlier generation, has returned with frightening immediacy. I do not make predictions. But I cannot ignore the danger, and I cannot separate it from the hope I inherited from parents who had already witnessed the devastation of global war. My writing for LA Progressive is one way of reflecting on this perilous world. It is also a way of refusing silence. I want to understand how authoritarianism gains its foothold, how democratic institutions become vulnerable, how political language can be turned against the very people it claims to represent, and how education might help recover the capacity for collective judgment. These are not new questions in my life. They are the questions that have followed me from the Jane-Finch Corridor to the university, from the classrooms of Henry Giroux to the intellectual community at Chapman, and from the conversations of international colleagues to the solitary act of writing at my desk. With Henry Giroux at Leon Trotsky’s grave in the garden of his home in Coyoacán, Mexico City. I have sometimes wondered what acquired wisdom actually means. It cannot simply be the accumulation of knowledge, the possession of degrees, or the retrospective arrangement of professional accomplishments. Nor can it mean that one has finally arrived at a place of certainty. The older I become, the more I recognize how much remains unresolved. Ideas that once seemed sufficient reveal their limitations. Convictions become more complex. The world refuses to conform to the categories through which we have tried to understand it. Perhaps acquired wisdom is less a destination than a willingness to remain answerable to the world—to keep learning, to question one's own assumptions, to recognize the humanity of others, and to resist the seductions of certainty when certainty becomes aninstrument of power. I think often about the children I taught in the Jane-Finch Corridor. I think about the young people whose lives were too easily described by the deficits of their neighbourhoodsrather than by the fullness of their humanity. I think about the teachers, students, colleagues, and friends who enlarged my intellectual life. I think about Henry Giroux's extraordinary lectures, the conversations around Freire at Chapman, the international encounters that unsettled my assumptions, and the correspondence that continues to deepen my understanding of theology and education. None of these experiences havesupplieda final answer. Together, they have taught me that education is a relationship with possibility. I also think about my parents and the generation that emerged from the Second World War. They had seen what human beings could do to one another. I was born into their hope that the world might never again descend into such a catastrophe. That hope has not disappeared. It has become more difficult to sustain, and therefore more necessary. I remain convinced that the task of critical education is to keep open the question of what human beings might become. It must expose the structures that diminish life, but it must also cultivate the imagination required to create something beyond them. Itmust be historically informed without becoming imprisoned by history, politically committed without becoming doctrinaire, and ethically grounded without surrendering its capacity for criticism. At this stage of my life, I no longer measure intellectual work primarily by the number of lectures delivered, conferences attended, or invitations accepted. I measure it by whether I can still contribute something meaningful to the conversation about the world we inhabit and the world we might yet create. I have not finished learning. I have not finished questioning. And I have not finished writing. The work remains unfinished because the world remains unfinished. At 78, I have come to understand that freedom is not a destination at which one finally arrives. It is an unfinished encounter with the world, with others, with God, and with the mysteries that remain beyond reach of our understanding. That, perhaps, is the wisdom I have acquired. Education Review
